description: Reivers, raids and the rough business of policing the Anglo-Scottish border, 1500–1603.
content_html:
The Border Landscape and Its People

The Anglo-Scottish border in the sixteenth century was not a fixed, clearly patrolled line but a lawless zone of upland moorland, shifting loyalties and endemic raiding. Border Reivers were the principal actors: families — Armstrongs, Elliots, Grahams, Nixons, Scotts — who raided across the border for cattle, sheep and ransomable prisoners with little distinction between English and Scottish victims. Reiver raids could strike at any time; a whole community’s livestock might vanish overnight. The practice was so embedded that it generated its own legal term: “blackmail” (originally protection money paid to reivers) and the phrase “bereaved” (to have been raided and robbed).

The borderlands were administered in three zones on each side: the West March, Middle March and East March. Each was governed by a Warden of the Marches, a powerful noble appointed by the Crown. Wardens held March Days — formal meetings at the border where disputes were settled and stolen goods returned. The system was supposed to provide order, but wardens were often themselves reiver clan members or in alliance with reiver families, making impartial enforcement difficult.

Key Fact

Border Reivers were raiding families from both sides of the Anglo-Scottish border. Wardens of the Marches were royal officials meant to enforce order, but their effectiveness was limited by their own connections to reiver families.

Warfare on the Borders: Flodden to Pinkie

Alongside the persistent low-level violence of reiving, the border region was also the site of pitched battles between English and Scottish armies. At Flodden in 1513, an English army under the Earl of Surrey defeated and killed James IV of Scotland and much of the Scottish nobility. Flodden was a catastrophe for Scotland — the king and thousands of men dead in a single afternoon — but it did not end the border problem. Scottish raiding continued, and English armies mounted periodic punitive invasions known as “rough wooings” in the 1540s, intended to force a marriage alliance between the young Mary Queen of Scots and the future Edward VI.

The Battle of Pinkie (1547) was one of the last major Anglo-Scottish engagements before the Union of Crowns. English forces defeated the Scots at Musselburgh in one of the first modern battles to combine massed infantry fire from handguns with cavalry and artillery. But military victory did not translate into political settlement. The Scots sought and received French support, and Mary was sent to France, frustrating English plans for a union by marriage. The border remained a zone of intermittent conflict throughout the mid-Tudor period.

For ordinary people in the border counties, warfare was a lived reality rather than a distant policy concern. Farms were attacked repeatedly; livestock — the main form of wealth in an upland pastoral economy — was the principal target. Communities built peel towers as refuges against raids. Wealthy families might negotiate arrangements with reiver clans, paying protection money (blackmail) rather than face repeated attack.

The violence was not simply chaotic. Reiving operated according to unwritten codes: taking goods was acceptable, killing without reason was not; ransoms were standard practice. The border community had developed its own semi-legal customs because the formal legal systems of England and Scotland were too distant and too slow to provide justice. This parallel informal legal culture was one reason the borderlands were so resistant to royal control throughout the sixteenth century.

The Union of Crowns and the End of Border Warfare

The Union of Crowns in 1603, when James VI of Scotland became James I of England, changed the border’s status fundamentally. What had been a frontier between two kingdoms became an internal region of a single Crown. James declared the border counties a “Middle Shires” and set about eliminating reiving through a sustained campaign of force. A joint Anglo-Scottish commission was established; reiver families faced hanging, transportation and the breaking up of their clans.

The Armstrong clan, one of the most powerful reiver families, was particularly targeted. Hundreds were executed or transported to Ireland in the early seventeenth century. By 1610, the pacification of the borders was largely complete. The border region, which had sustained a distinctive culture of violence and semi-independence for centuries, was integrated into the wider political and legal order of Britain within a decade of the union. The speed of this change illustrates how the border had been sustained as a lawless zone largely by the existence of two competing state authorities — remove the frontier and the reivers had nowhere left to operate.

The Anglo-Scottish border was never simply a local problem — it was part of the wider strategic competition between England, Scotland and France. Scotland’s alliance with France (the “Auld Alliance”) meant that a hostile Scotland represented a second front against England whenever England was at war with France. Henry VIII’s Italian wars, for example, were accompanied by Scottish raiding that culminated at Flodden (1513). Securing the northern border was therefore an ongoing strategic priority for Tudor governments.

The Rough Wooing policy of the 1540s — trying to force Scotland into a Protestant union with England through military pressure — failed diplomatically but contributed to a gradual shift in Scottish elite opinion towards England in the later sixteenth century. Protestant reformers in Scotland looked to England for support against French Catholic influence. Elizabeth’s tacit support for Scottish Protestants in 1559–60 helped install a Protestant regime in Edinburgh — making the eventual Union of Crowns possible.

Key Fact

The Union of Crowns (1603) ended border reiving by removing the frontier that had sustained it. James VI/I declared the borderlands ‘Middle Shires’ and used a joint Anglo-Scottish commission to execute, imprison and transport reiver families. The Armstrongs and other major clans were broken within a decade.
exam_tip_html: For Change and Continuity essays, border warfare is an excellent example of continuity across time — reiving persisted for over a century despite state efforts to control it — followed by rapid change once the political context shifted with the Union of Crowns. Examiners reward students who explain why the change happened when it did, not just that it happened. For Explain Why questions, practise linking specific detail (March Days, peel towers, Armstrongs) to broader patterns (limits of royal authority, the role of geography and divided sovereignty).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Border Reivers raided both sides of the Anglo-Scottish frontier for over a century. The Wardens of the Marches were meant to enforce order but were often too embedded in border society to be effective.
  • Pitched battles — Flodden (1513) and Pinkie (1547) — demonstrated English military superiority but could not settle the border question, which was also bound up with the Franco-Scottish alliance.
  • The Union of Crowns in 1603 ended border warfare rapidly by removing the frontier itself. James VI/I’s pacification of the ‘Middle Shires’ broke the major reiver clans within a decade.

practice_questions.text: Give one reason why the Wardens of the Marches found it difficult to stop border reiving.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: precise reason with accurate detail (e.g. wardens were often from or allied with reiver families themselves, making impartial enforcement of border law difficult). Developing: vague (e.g. 'they were far away').

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of border warfare on people living in the border region.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. repeated raids on farms took livestock, the main form of wealth; communities built peel towers as fortified refuges against attack. Developing: identifies impacts without detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Union of Crowns (1603) was so effective in ending border reiving.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — explains how removing the frontier (which had sustained reiving by creating divided authority) allowed a joint commission to operate, how James systematically targeted major clans (Armstrongs), and why the speed of pacification reveals the political roots of the problem. Secure: Clear argument with two or more reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Flodden (1513) was significant for Anglo-Scottish relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — covers immediate impact (James IV killed, Scottish nobility devastated), strategic significance (Scotland unable to raid effectively for a generation), and limits (border problem continued, Scottish alliance with France persisted). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How far did the Anglo-Scottish border remain ungovernable in the period c.1500–c.1603? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — balances evidence of persistence (reiving despite March Day system, Wardens compromised, peel towers as evidence of endemic threat) against evidence of partial order (March Days did function, Flodden showed English military reach) and the eventual rapid change post-1603; reaches a sustained evidenced judgement. Secure: Clear argument covering both sides. Developing: Mostly one-sided. Emerging: Simple points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why border warfare was connected to England's wider foreign policy during the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis — links the Auld Alliance (Scotland-France) to the two-front strategic problem for English kings; shows how Flodden (1513) coincided with Henry VIII's French campaign; connects Rough Wooing (1540s) to Tudor policy of forcing a Protestant union; explains how Elizabeth's support for Scottish Protestants eventually removed the threat. Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence. Developing: Some argument. Emerging: Simple points.

options: A Scottish victory that forced England to pay tribute

flashcard_questions.q: What were Wardens of the Marches?

glossary_terms.definition: Families from the Anglo-Scottish borderlands who conducted raids on both sides of the border for livestock, goods and ransom in the sixteenth century.
Royal officials appointed to administer justice and enforce order in each of the three March zones on the English and Scottish sides of the border.
Fortified stone tower-houses used by border families as refuges against raider attacks.
The transformation of the former Anglo-Scottish borderlands into a pacified 'Middle Shires' region after the Union of Crowns in 1603, achieved through the suppression of the reiver clans.
